claims.text: Crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by competition between mixing entropy and kinetically limited atomic diffusion during rapid heating and cooling.
Small differences in atomic mobility among the constituent noble metals can drive or suppress local elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching can kinetically preserve a metastable single-phase state.
Diffusivity differences can produce microheterogeneities that predispose the nanoparticles to phase separation.
A 10-minute intermediate thermal hold at approximately 70–80% of the lowest constituent melting temperature can allow differential atomic transport to equilibrate local composition.
Heating rates on the order of 10^3 K/min followed by immediate quenching provide kinetic trapping in the baseline process.
Local elemental diffusivities and segregation kinetics mediate whether a uniform metastable solid solution or incipient elemental clustering forms.
The annealing hold increases atomic mobility.
Increased mobility during the hold can alleviate local compositional fluctuations and permit broader sampling of configurational space.
A high nucleation rate during rapid processing traps the elemental distribution.
The annealing hold steers the system toward a thermodynamically favored, uniform single-phase structure through transient atomic rearrangement.
The annealing hold reduces uncontrolled elemental segregation.
The annealing hold reduces morphological anisotropy.
Annealed samples will exhibit greater phase homogeneity than immediately quenched baseline samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit less elemental segregation than immediately quenched baseline samples.
Annealed samples will have more controlled and uniform nanoparticle morphology than immediately quenched baseline samples.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal high-entropy alloys whose constituents have relatively similar atomic radii and chemical characteristics but modest diffusivity differences.
The proposed mechanism is limited to compositions having sufficiently high mixing entropy to favor single-phase formation.
If constituent diffusivities differ too strongly, the intermediate hold may itself cause residual segregation.
